content: High-priority variables in the context of violence against women (VAW) include both the recurrence of violence experienced by survivors and the likelihood of repeat offenses by perpetrators. It is essential to have a detailed understanding of the local context to evaluate whether collecting such additional variables might deter individuals from seeking services or inadvertently cause harm. Most administrative data systems do not differentiate between biological sex and gender identity, often combining them into a single variable. Consequently, the term female or woman is typically assumed to refer to cisgender women, meaning individuals whose gender identity aligns with their sex assigned at birth. However, some countries are advancing efforts to identify transgender and non-binary individuals in surveys and administrative data collection. International standards for capturing gender identity are also evolving, as highlighted by UNECE (2019) and UNODC/UN Women (2022). The high prevalence of gender-based violence among gender minorities underscores the importance of designing administrative data systems that better address the needs of these survivors and the support they receive. When safe and legally permissible, it is crucial to document gender identity as a separate variable, including response options for cisgender, transgender, and non-binary individuals. For guidance, refer to UNODC and UN Women (2022). Argentina provides an example of counting VAW services and survivors through its administrative data systems. A survivor-centered approach is a fundamental principle in collecting and using VAW administrative data. This technical guidance emphasizes involving civil society organizations (CSOs) that work closely with survivors, as well as survivors themselves, in the design and governance of these systems. While it is commendable to include survivors' voices by regularly asking them to assess service quality, this must be balanced with ensuring their safety and access to services. Survivors often face power imbalances with service providers, and these services are critical to their well-being. Standardized exit surveys may not yield meaningful feedback for quality improvement, as responses are often overly positive when collected in the service delivery context or by representatives of the service-providing organization. To preserve confidentiality and avoid jeopardizing survivors' relationships with service providers, this guidance recommends alternative methods for gathering feedback. These include informing all service users about complaint mechanisms and opportunities to provide anonymous feedback through ombudspersons, professional oversight bodies, anonymous complaint boxes, or online platforms. Additionally, research on survivors' experiences with services, conducted by trained researchers following approved protocols, can complement administrative data. Observational research by independent researchers at service delivery sites and qualitative research, such as interviews with survivors conducted outside the service setting, are also valuable. Engaging CSOs as collaborators in participatory action research and involving advocates and survivor organizations in data coordination mechanisms can further enhance the process. The technical expertise of National Statistical Offices (NSOs) can be instrumental in establishing and documenting standards for data collection and management, including the creation of metadata for all variables. Metadata should include operational definitions, data sources, reporting frequency, response categories, and limitations. Understanding the context of data production by different institutions and service providers is critical for accurate interpretation and communication of the data. Key considerations include the time period of the VAW incidents being reported and the stage of the investigation at which the data is recorded. For example, police data may focus on specific incidents, while specialized services may collect information on ongoing or past violence. Tools are available to guide the production of metadata for administrative sources. For the recommended minimum VAW administrative data set, this guidance identifies response options and discusses the advantages and disadvantages of using the case report or the individual as the unit of count. Standardizing response options across sectors requires analyzing existing data and agreeing on classification or coding options. Behavioral definitions of VAW, which focus on acts committed by the perpetrator against the survivor, allow for standardized data categories across settings. These definitions can make forms of VAW visible even if they are not criminalized, contributing to the realization of international human rights standards. Recording all types of VAW using behavioral definitions aims to improve recognition of these forms of violence by survivors and service providers, ultimately leading to better laws, policies, and programs. However, cultural norms and legal definitions influence what types of VAW are reported and recorded, with less recognized or criminalized forms likely being underreported. The basic unit of count for VAW administrative data is the case report. Concerns about double counting survivors can be addressed by recognizing that multiple visits to different services reflect the number of reports made and the services sought, rather than duplication. Unique identifiers within service delivery sites or across sectors can help track survivors and perpetrators over time, enabling a deeper understanding of VAW interventions and outcomes. Linked data sets, such as those between health and police sectors, can provide insights into referrals, service utilization, and case progression. Argentina's VAW law exemplifies the integration of inter-jurisdictional and inter-institutional registries to collect administrative data on VAW. The Unified Registry of Cases of Violence Against Women (RUCVM) collects a minimum data set, including age, sex, gender identity, and unique identifiers, to develop comprehensive statistics and inform policy responses.
